issues.legal_issue: An appellate court may reverse an acquittal when the trial court’s view is not reasonably possible and the evidence establishes guilt beyond reasonable doubt.
material_facts: The trial court acquitted the accused after treating discrepancies in the evidence as grounds for doubt.
The High Court reappreciated the evidence and reversed the acquittal.

The Supreme Court found that the trial court had taken a hyper-technical view of minor contradictions and that the evidence, read as a whole, established the accused persons’ presence, participation and responsibility for the death.
issues.conclusion: The High Court was justified in reversing the acquittal, and the Supreme Court upheld the conviction and sentence.
issues.legal_principle: Under Dwarka Dass v. State of Haryana (2003) 1 SCC 204, an appellate court should not interfere with an acquittal merely because it prefers another reasonable view. Under Narinder Singh v. State of Punjab, 2000 Crl. LJ 3462 (SC), it may reappreciate the evidence where the acquitting court’s view was not possible, perverse, infirm or palpably erroneous, or involved material irregularity. Guilt must be proved beyond reasonable doubt, as explained in State of U.P. v. Krishna Gopal (1988) 4 SCC 302 and Gurbachan Singh v. Satpal Singh (1990) 1 SCC 445.

predicates.appeal_against_acquittal: The proceeding is an appeal challenging an acquittal.
predicates.trial_view_not_reasonably_possible: The trial court adopted a view of the evidence that was not reasonably possible.
predicates.trial_view_based_on_material_error: The trial court materially erred, for example by treating minor discrepancies as decisive or overlooking material evidence.
predicates.evidence_proves_guilt_beyond_reasonable_: The evidence, considered as a whole, proves the accused’s guilt beyond reasonable doubt.

issues.definition: When an appeal challenges an acquittal, the acquittal rests on a materially erroneous or unavailable view, and the evidence proves guilt beyond reasonable doubt, appellate interference is justified.

issues.legal_issue: Minor discrepancies and omissions do not require rejection of eyewitness testimony when they do not materially affect the core of the prosecution case and the testimony is trustworthy.
material_facts: The eyewitnesses differed on the sequence of shots and who fired at whom.

The Supreme Court found that the discrepancies did not undermine the central account that the accused were present, an altercation occurred, shots were fired, and the deceased died from the injuries inflicted.
Other witnesses and medical evidence supported the principal parts of the eyewitness account.
issues.conclusion: The discrepancies did not justify rejecting the eyewitness evidence or finding that the prosecution had failed to prove its case.
issues.legal_principle: Leela Ram v. State of Haryana (1999) 9 SCC 525 permits a court to separate reliable evidence from exaggerations or embellishments. Sunil Kumar Sambhudayal Gupta (Dr.) v. State of Maharashtra (2010) 13 SCC 657 explains that minor contradictions, inconsistencies and improvements that do not affect the core of the case are not grounds to reject evidence, while contradictions going to the root of the case may undermine it. The court also relied on State of Rajasthan v. Kalki, Syed Ibrahim v. State of A.P., Arumugam v. State, and the other decisions discussed in Sunil Kumar Sambhudayal Gupta.

rule.if: criminal_prosecution and eyewitnesses_give_core_account and discrepancies_do_not_materially_affect_core and testimony_is_supported_by_other_evidence

predicates.criminal_prosecution: The proceeding is a criminal prosecution in which the prosecution relies on eyewitness testimony.
predicates.eyewitnesses_give_core_account: Eyewitnesses describe the central events and the accused’s involvement.
predicates.discrepancies_do_not_materially_affect_c: Differences or omissions in the accounts do not materially undermine the central prosecution case.
predicates.testimony_is_supported_by_other_evidence: Other evidence supports the principal parts of the eyewitness account.

issues.definition: In a criminal prosecution, eyewitness testimony is not rejected for minor discrepancies when it gives a reliable account of the central events, the differences do not affect that account, and other evidence supports it.

issues.legal_issue: Ocular evidence may be relied on when medical evidence supports its principal features and does not make it impossible.
material_facts: The medical evidence disclosed injuries to the injured witness and the deceased.
The Supreme Court found that those injuries were consistent with the principal parts of the eyewitness testimony.
issues.conclusion: The ocular evidence could not be rejected on the basis of the asserted inconsistencies because the medical evidence supported its principal features.
issues.legal_principle: Under Rakesh v. State of M.P. (2011) 9 SCC 698, ocular evidence ordinarily has primacy over medical evidence unless the medical evidence makes the ocular account improbable or completely rules out the possibility that it is true. The Court also referred to State of U.P. v. Hari Chand, Abdul Sayeed v. State of M.P., and Bhajan Singh v. State of Haryana.

predicates.criminal_prosecution: The proceeding is a criminal prosecution in which the prosecution relies on oral eyewitness evidence.
predicates.ocular_evidence_describes_injuries: Eyewitnesses describe an occurrence and injuries caused during it.
predicates.medical_evidence_supports_principal_feat: Medical evidence is consistent with the principal features of the eyewitness account.
predicates.medical_evidence_does_not_rule_out_ocula: Medical evidence does not make the eyewitness account impossible.

issues.definition: In a criminal prosecution, ocular evidence describing injuries may be relied on when medical evidence supports its principal features and does not make the account impossible.

issues.legal_issue: An eyewitness’s unusual reaction to a crime does not justify rejecting the testimony unless the reaction affects the prosecution case.
material_facts: The injured eyewitness ran from the scene, entered a room and locked himself inside, and later returned to the scene.
The Supreme Court found that this conduct did not affect the prosecution account of the occurrence.
issues.conclusion: The eyewitness’s unusual conduct did not undermine the prosecution case and was not a basis for rejecting his evidence.
issues.legal_principle: Appabhai v. State of Gujarat, 1988 Supp SCC 241, and Rana Pratap v. State of Haryana recognize that witnesses may react differently to a crime and that there is no fixed pattern of natural reaction. A court should assess whether the reaction affects the prosecution story rather than reject testimony merely because the reaction was unusual.

predicates.criminal_prosecution: The proceeding is a criminal prosecution in which the prosecution relies on an eyewitness.
predicates.eyewitness_reacts_unusually: An eyewitness behaves in a way that may appear unusual after witnessing the crime.
predicates.reaction_does_not_affect_prosecution_acc: The eyewitness’s reaction does not undermine or otherwise affect the prosecution account of the occurrence.

issues.definition: In a criminal prosecution, an eyewitness’s unusual reaction is not a basis to reject the testimony when the reaction does not affect the prosecution account.

issues.legal_issue: Eyewitnesses’ failure to identify recovered weapons does not defeat the prosecution case when the recovery evidence and the evidence as a whole remain reliable.
material_facts: The eyewitnesses did not identify the weapons shown to them at trial as the weapons used in the incident.
A witness to the recoveries described the recovery of the weapons at the accused’s instance and identified them in court.
The Supreme Court found, on considering all the evidence, that the failure of the eyewitnesses to recognize the weapons made no difference to the prosecution case.
issues.conclusion: The eyewitnesses’ failure to identify the recovered weapons did not undermine the prosecution case.
issues.legal_principle: The Court accepted that, in the circumstances, the recovery witness’s evidence could be relied on for identification of the recovered weapons and that the eyewitnesses might not have clearly seen them amid the commotion. It distinguished Mahendra Pratap Singh v. State of U.P. (2009) 11 SCC 334, where the evidence as a whole did not inspire confidence and two views were possible.

predicates.criminal_prosecution: The proceeding is a criminal prosecution in which the prosecution relies on recovered weapons as evidence.
predicates.eyewitnesses_do_not_identify_recovered_w: Eyewitnesses do not identify the weapons shown in court as those used in the crime.
predicates.recovery_evidence_identifies_weapons: Evidence about the recovery identifies the weapons and connects their recovery to the accused.
predicates.remaining_evidence_supports_prosecution_: The remaining evidence, considered as a whole, supports the prosecution account.

issues.definition: In a criminal prosecution, eyewitnesses’ failure to identify recovered weapons does not defeat the prosecution case when recovery evidence identifies the weapons and the remaining evidence supports the prosecution account.
